title: Neuroception
definition: The nervous system's continuous, automatic evaluation of safety and threat, operating below conscious awareness.
summary: Coined by Stephen Porges, neuroception describes how the nervous system scans the environment and internal states to determine: Is this safe, dangerous, or life-threatening? This evaluation happens before conscious thought and shapes what emotions, perceptions, and behaviors become available.

content.title: What It Is
content.content: Neuroception is the nervous system's below-conscious threat detection system. It continuously evaluates three types of signals: exteroceptive (external sensory input), interoceptive (internal body states), and memory-based (pattern-matched associations from past experience). Based on this evaluation, the system prepares the body for engagement, defense, or shutdown — all before conscious awareness begins.

content.title: How TEG-Blue Maps It
content.content: Neuroception is the mechanism that determines position on the Four-Mode Gradient. When neuroception reads safety, the system moves toward Connection. When it reads threat, the system moves toward Protection. Crucially, neuroception evaluates experienced safety, not objective danger — a stimulus that is objectively safe can trigger threat response if it matches patterns associated with past danger. This explains why 'knowing better' doesn't change reaction.

content.title: Research Basis
content.content: Term coined by Stephen Porges as part of Polyvagal Theory. Porges, S. W. (2004). Neuroception: A subconscious system for detecting threats and safety. Zero to Three, 24(5), 19-24. The concept integrates with LeDoux's work on subcortical threat processing and Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis.
